title: Words from Japan
kidRule: Words from Japanese are usually spelled just the way they sound, one clear beat at a time, and most beats end in a vowel, like KA-RA-TE!
hint: This word came from Japan. Clap it out one beat at a time. Which vowel do you hear at the end of each beat?
reminder: Japanese words are spelled beat by beat, and most beats end in a plain vowel: A, I, U, E, or O. An 'ee' sound at the end is usually the letter I.

check.question: Why does ORIGAMI end with the letter I and not the letter Y?
check.correctAnswer: It came from Japanese, and Japanese words usually end their beats with a plain vowel like I!
distractors: Because Y is never allowed at the end of a word
Because every word about paper ends with the letter I

words.def: A Japanese sport where you learn special kicks, punches, and blocks.
words.sent: My brother earned a yellow belt in karate.
words.story: In Japanese, karate means 'empty hand', because you do it with no weapons at all!
words.card: The *rat* earned a black belt in *karate* and bowed to the cat!

words.def: The Japanese art of folding paper into shapes like birds and frogs.
words.sent: We made a paper crane in origami class.
words.story: In Japanese, 'ori' means folding and 'kami' means paper, so origami means 'folding paper'!
words.card: I *am* folding an *origami* frog that can really hop!

words.def: A tiny picture, like a smiley face, that you can put in a message.
words.sent: I sent Grandpa a laughing emoji.
words.story: This word is Japanese: 'e' means picture and 'moji' means letter. The first sets were made in Japan in the 1990s!
words.card: Each *emoji* giggled when I sent th*em* to Grandma!

words.def: A long Japanese robe with wide sleeves, tied with a wide belt.
words.sent: She wore a silk kimono covered with cherry blossoms.
words.story: In Japanese, kimono simply means 'a thing to wear'!
words.card: The cat put *on* a silky *kimono* and danced in the garden!

words.def: A tiny tree grown in a small pot and trimmed to keep it little.
words.sent: Grandma trims her bonsai with tiny scissors.
words.story: In Japanese, bonsai means 'planted in a tray', and some of these little trees are hundreds of years old!
words.card: The ladybug sat *on* the *bonsai* and felt like a giant!

words.def: A sweet and salty sauce, or food that is grilled with that sauce.
words.sent: We had chicken teriyaki with rice for dinner.
words.story: In Japanese, 'teri' means shine and 'yaki' means grilled, because the sauce makes the food glossy!
words.card: The *yak* ordered *teriyaki* noodles with extra napkins!

words.def: A number puzzle where you fill a grid so every row, column, and box has each number just once.
words.sent: Grandma solves a sudoku puzzle every morning.
words.story: The name is short for a Japanese saying that means 'the numbers must stay single'!
words.card: *Do* you think a *sudoku* puzzle dreams about numbers at night?

words.def: A very short poem from Japan with just three lines.
words.sent: I wrote a haiku about the first snowy day.
words.story: A haiku has only three lines, with 5, 7, and 5 beats. Many of them are about nature and the seasons!
words.card: *Ha* *ha*! My *haiku* about a sneezing frog made the teacher laugh!

words.def: A giant ocean wave, usually started by an earthquake under the sea.
words.sent: Scientists can warn people before a tsunami reaches the shore.
words.card: My rubber duck made a tiny bathtub *tsunami* and then dried off in the *sun*!

words.def: A fun activity where you sing along to music while the words show on a screen.
words.sent: Dad sang a silly song at the karaoke party.
words.story: In Japanese, karaoke means 'empty orchestra', because the band is missing and you are the singer!
words.card: Is it *ok* if my goldfish sings *karaoke* tonight?
